transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-04 14:30 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neal (Archer Head of ML), Sofia Ruiz (Platform Eng), Daniel Park (CTO)

Summary (auto): Cost/econ focused discovery; Archer wants predictable unit costs without sacrificing 99th pctl latency for customer-facing completions.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood, ravi and i will run through cost/usability questions today, did i get the right folks?
[00:06] Liam: yeah this is liam, head of ml, thanks. sofia and daniel here too.
[00:12] Maya: cool, quick agenda — a few questions about your workload, then walk through per-token pricing and levers (batching, kv/prefix cache, quant), and then next steps. sound good?
[00:18] Daniel: yep, go ahead.

[01:02] Ravi: to ground this, can you share rough qps and prompt/response lengths? even ballparks help with sizing.
[01:12] Sofia: sure. right now internal staging shows ~6 rps peak, expected to grow to ~30 rps in three months. median prompt ~120 tokens, median completion ~220 tokens, but customer-facing flows hit 600 tokens in long mode.
[01:28] Liam: important: 99th pctl latency target is 450ms for short flows, up to 1.2s ok for longer ones. Budget — we're looking at roughly $20k-30k/mo for inference costs initially.

[02:11] Maya: great, that's helpful. so two immediate levers: model choice / quantization and serving mode (hosted vs dedicated). for hosted we have predictable per-token rates, no infra to manage; dedicated gives better unit cost at scale but requires reserved commit.
[02:29] Liam: can you quantify the per-token delta? like how much cheaper is dedicated per token?
[02:36] Maya: rough examples — for a 13B-type open model on hosted, think $0.XX per 1k tokens (note: speaker says cents and numbers get fuzzy) — um sorry, example numbers: hosted might be $0.8 / 1k input + $1.6 / 1k output for certain models; that obviously varies by model family. on Dedicated with a reserved pool and batching/kv cache, we typically see 30-60% lower per-token spend depending on utilization and batchability.
[03:05] Ravi: adding to that — if you can batch well and use prefix or kv caching for repeated prompts (chat history reuse), effective tokens served drop because cache hits bypass decoding work. for customer flows with repeated system prompts we often get 20-40% effective savings.
[03:22] Sofia: ok, what's the tradeoff on latency when batching? our 99th pctl is tight.
[03:29] Ravi: good q — there's a latency vs throughput tradeoff. continuous batching in our runtime tries to keep tail latency under SLOs by using dynamic batch windows; at low qps batching size is small, so latency impact minimal. at high qps you get more batching -> lower cost but slightly higher median latency. you can configure constraints and use dedicated capacity to reduce that impact.
[03:58] Liam: the KV cache — is that the same as prefix cache? how stateful is it, and does it add network hops?
[04:06] Maya: KV cache is the internal key-value cache for transformer kv states — prefix caching is a higher-level optimization where we cache whole prefix outputs for repeated prompts. for hosted, cache is regional and managed; for private/dedicated you can have more control, and warm-up is faster if you pin models. there can be some network overhead but it's usually small compared to decode time.

[05:31] Daniel: for Dedicated commits, what kind of minimums and commit terms do you have? we can't justify huge annual commits right now.
[05:40] Maya: typical dedicated starts at modest commitments — we can do monthly reserved pools with discounts versus pay-as-you-go; there's flexibility. for enterprise private/on-prem we talk larger minimums. we'll send specific pricing tiers after this call.
[05:55] Liam: can you run me through an example calc — say 1M requests per month, avg tokens per request 300, what's the spend difference hosted vs dedicated?
[06:06] Ravi: sure — rough calc: 1M * 300 tokens = 300M tokens. if hosted effective blended is $0.002 per token (example), that's $600k. with dedicated and batching plus cache we might drive to $0.0009 per token -> $270k. that's a big swing, but the key is utilization — if your pool is underutilized the math changes.
[06:35] Sofia: those numbers seem high; our budget is 25k/mo not 270k. we won't be at 1M requests.
[06:42] Maya: understood — this is why model selection and prompt engineering matter. for many customers we recommend 7B/13B quantized variants for high-volume lower-latency flows. also edge caching of embeddings for rerank helps reduce generation calls.

[07:20] Liam: what's the uplift of moving from FP16 to 4-bit quant? accuracy hit?
[07:27] Ravi: depends on model; for many Llama-style open models 4-bit (q4) loses a couple percent on some evals but is fine for lots of assistant tasks. we provide quant profiles and recommend running eval prompts — we can include quality-vs-cost curves in the spreadsheet.
[07:45] Daniel: how do you measure effective unit cost when considering cached hits? we need a sane way to show dollars per meaningful response.
[07:53] Maya: we report tokens served, cache-hit rates, and "effective tokens per response" — our console shows token-level cost breakdowns including cache hit savings; we can map that to dollars per success metric you care about.

[09:00] Sofia: sample architecture question — if we use private (VPC) deployment, do you still handle autoscaling and batching?
[09:10] Maya: for Private we run a customer-managed control plane model; autoscaling is supported but with different ops responsibilities. Dedicated (hosted dedicated pool) gives you the managed autoscale with redwood control plane and SLA. Private on-prem has more handshakes. security controls like KMS and audit logs are supported across both.

[10:12] Liam: ok, we need to get an apples-to-apples cost model: include model family, token rates, cache assumptions, batching assumptions, and utilization. can you provide a template?
[10:20] Maya: yes we'll send a spreadsheet template. we'll need your traffic profile and which flows are latency-critical vs background.

[11:05] Ravi: small tip — if you can separate hot paths (short completions) from background long jobs, you can route hot paths to low-latency Dedicated pools and long jobs to cheaper preemptible or batch workers; that cuts cost significantly.
[11:22] Liam: do you support preemptible nodes or cheaper tiers?
[11:27] Maya: yes — burst and spot-like capacity is available for non-critical workloads; for critical SLOs we keep them off spot.

[12:00] Sofia: on security, we'll need SOC2, SAML SSO, and KMS integration. is that readily available?
[12:08] Maya: yes, SOC2 attestation, SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations are in our security pack; we'll attach the security deck.

[13:33] Daniel: real concern — benching: how do we run realistic benchmarks? can your SE run the benchmark on Dedicated with our prompts?
[13:42] Ravi: absolutely — we do pilots. typical pilot: 1-2 weeks, we provision a small dedicated pool, run your prompt sets, measure latency and cost under your traffic shape. we provide a benchmark report.

[14:20] Liam: what's the onboarding time for pilot? we are short on cycles.
[14:25] Ravi: 3-5 business days to stand up a pilot if we have the prompt set and traffic profile. we'll need a contact who can share sample prompts and auth for a short-lived dataset.

[15:00] Maya: just flagging one more lever — model routing. you can route high-priority traffic to larger models for quality and lower-cost models for bulk tasks. that hybrid approach often fits constrained budgets.

[16:10] Sofia: question on billing granularity — do you bill by token or by compute seconds? we need clear unit economics for forecasting.
[16:18] Maya: hosted billing is per token; dedicated reserved pools are monthly capacity commitments plus usage adjustments; we give effective dollars per token in reporting and you can export token-level logs. we'll include an example invoice.

[17:00] Liam: are there hidden costs around egress or data storage?
[17:05] Maya: for hosted, typical egress is minimal for text workloads; for private/on-prem there are network considerations. log retention beyond default window is an add-on. we'll call those out.

[18:20] Daniel: okay — say we can commit $25k/mo — what performance can we expect?
[18:28] Ravi: depends on model; for $25k month on dedicated that might map to a small reserved pool supporting low 2-digit rps for 13B-like models with aggressive batching. if you need sub-500ms 99th for short completions, you may need to allocate more to reduce batching delay or use smaller models optimized for latency.

[19:05] Liam: do you have customers who've done this split routing and seen cost halved?
[19:11] Maya: yes — several fintechs route 80% background to cheaper models and 20% hot path to low-latency; they're often able to reduce spend 40-60% vs naive hosted usage. we'll anonymize case examples in the follow-up.

[20:00] Sofia: about quantization — do you provide pre-quantized artifacts or do we need to do it?
[20:05] Ravi: we provide quantized variants and guidance; for Private you might run custom quant steps, but we support shipping recommended q4/q5 artifacts for many open models.

[21:17] Liam: any gotchas around prompt engineering that materially impacts tokens?
[21:22] Maya: yes — system prompts that repeat full context each turn drive tokens. using prefix or stateful conversation reduces that. also compressing system instructions and using embeddings + retrieval for factual context cut prompt length.

[22:45] Daniel: we will need an internal ROI doc for execs — can you provide a short one pager showing expected savings by routing and batching?
[22:52] Maya: yes we'll include a one-pager with numbers and assumptions.

[24:10] (brief cross talk — everyone confirming deliverables)

[25:00] Ravi: for the pilot, can you confirm 3 flows and sample size?
[25:05] Sofia: we'll provide 3 representative flows: auth chat (short), customer-summary (medium), long-report (long). sample sizes ~500 each for initial run.

[26:20] Liam: timeline — we'd like pilot mid-march, decision late march if numbers align.

[27:15] Maya: sounds good. to summarize next steps: we send cost template + security deck + quant profiles; you send prompts and traffic profile; we stand up pilot and run benchmarks.

[28:02] Daniel: quick question — how do you account for model updates? if we pin a version for pilot do you support seamless rollovers?
[28:12] Maya: yes, our rollout tool supports canaries and automatic fallback to pinned variants. Private deployments can use same rollout semantics with slightly different ops.

[30:00] (silence / note taking)

[31:10] Liam: around SLA — do you have uptime SLAs for dedicated?
[31:16] Maya: yes for Dedicated we have SLA-backed targets, we'll include the SLA doc.

[32:00] Sofia: one last operational thing — observability — can we get token-level breakdowns per route?

[32:07] Ravi: yes console gives per-route token usage, latency histograms, and cost attribution. you can export for internal chargeback.

[34:00] (wrap up)

[34:10] Maya: ok thanks all. we'll send the follow-ups by friday. any final q?

[34:18] Daniel: none from me.

[34:20] Liam: nope. thanks.

[34:25] Sofia: thanks.

[34:30] Maya: great, talk soon. bye.
file_notes: Transcript contains minor transcription errors and shorthand; product names and numbers are approximations for discussion; follow-up will include precise pricing tiers.
